final_answer:
Let
\[
y\equiv 2-x \pmod {p^n}.
\]
Then each valid \(x\) determines exactly one \(y\), so \(M_n(p)\) is the number of \(x\pmod {p^n}\) satisfying
\[
x^2\equiv (2-x)^3\pmod {p^n}.
\]
Expanding,
\[
x^2-(2-x)^3=x^3-5x^2+12x-8=(x-1)(x^2-4x+8).
\]
So we must count
\[
(x-1)(x^2-4x+8)\equiv0\pmod {p^n}.
\]

If \(p\ne5\), the two factors cannot both be divisible by \(p\), since at \(x\equiv1\pmod p\),
\[
x^2-4x+8\equiv 1-4+8=5\not\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Thus the product is \(0\pmod {p^n}\) exactly when one factor is \(0\pmod {p^n}\).

The linear factor gives one solution:
\[
x\equiv1\pmod {p^n}.
\]
For the quadratic,
\[
x^2-4x+8=(x-2)^2+4,
\]
so it is solvable iff
\[
(x-2)^2\equiv -4\pmod {p^n},
\]
equivalently iff \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). Therefore it contributes \(2\) solutions if \(L_p=1\), and \(0\) solutions if \(L_p=-1\). Hence for \(p\ne5\),
\[
M_n(p)=1+\begin{cases}2,&L_p=1,\\0,&L_p=-1,\end{cases}=2+L_p.
\]

It remains to handle \(p=5\). Put
\[
t=x-1.
\]
Then
\[
x^2-4x+8=t^2-2t+5,
\]
so we count
\[
t(t^2-2t+5)\equiv0\pmod {5^n}.
\]
Modulo \(5\),
\[
t^2-2t+5\equiv t(t-2),
\]
so the roots lie in the residue classes \(t\equiv0\) and \(t\equiv2\pmod5\).

By Hensel lifting, \(t^2-2t+5\) has one root \(\alpha\equiv0\pmod5\) and one root \(\beta\equiv2\pmod5\) modulo \(5^n\). Also \(\alpha\) has exact \(5\)-adic valuation \(1\), since
\[
\alpha(\alpha-2)=-5
\]
and \(\alpha-2\) is a unit.

The class \(t\equiv2\pmod5\) contributes exactly one solution, namely \(t\equiv\beta\pmod {5^n}\).

In the class \(t\equiv0\pmod5\), the factor \(t-\beta\) is a unit, so we need
\[
v_5(t)+v_5(t-\alpha)\ge n.
\]
For \(n=1\), this gives one residue class, \(t\equiv0\pmod5\). Together with \(t\equiv2\), this gives
\[
M_1(5)=2.
\]

For \(n=2\), every \(t\equiv0\pmod5\) satisfies both \(v_5(t)\ge1\) and \(v_5(t-\alpha)\ge1\), giving \(5\) residues modulo \(25\). Together with the \(\beta\)-root,
\[
M_2(5)=6.
\]

For \(n\ge3\), the condition in the \(t\equiv0\) class is equivalent to
\[
t\equiv0\pmod {5^{n-1}}
\quad\text{or}\quad
t\equiv\alpha\pmod {5^{n-1}}.
\]
Each congruence gives \(5\) residues modulo \(5^n\), and they are disjoint because \(v_5(\alpha)=1<n-1\). Thus this class contributes \(10\) solutions, and the \(\beta\)-root contributes one more:
\[
M_n(5)=11\qquad(n\ge3).
\]

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
M_n(p)=
\begin{cases}
2+L_p,& p\ne5,\\
2,& p=5,\ n=1,\\
6,& p=5,\ n=2,\\
11,& p=5,\ n\ge3.
\end{cases}
}
\]
